title: Social media sharing of low-quality news sources by political elites
screen_reason: Behavioural Twitter study of 3.4 million tweets by members of the US Congress, the German Bundestag and the British parliament (2016-01-01 to 2022-03-16), in which every external link was matched to NewsGuard's domain ratings and links to domains scoring under 60 were classified 'not trustworthy'. The paper reports the proportion of shared links that are untrustworthy, broken down by party (Republicans 3.86%, Democrats 0.43%, CDU/CSU 0.18%, SPD 0.03%, Tory 0.25%, Labour 0.05%) - shares of shared links carrying unreliable sources with defined denominators, i.e. SHARING (content_share) per §3. Party breakdowns are the paper's headline, which §2 explicitly allows as rows.

estimates.ground_truth_detail: NewsGuard domain ratings: score <60 = not trustworthy. The authors describe this as a trustworthiness assessment by professional fact checkers of the domain a link points to (their sentence is split across the PDF's columns, hence paraphrased here), and note that as of March 2022 NewsGuard indexed 6,860 English and 145 German-language domains, of which 62.8% (English) and 74.5% (German) are considered trustworthy. Classification is at DOMAIN level, not item level. Validation: the authors checked whether major outlets are missing from the database and whether the missing ones are politically biased, and reproduced the main result with an independently compiled list of untrustworthy domains built from academic and journalistic fact-checking sites (Supplementary Tables S4-S5), which gives higher levels but the same trend.
estimates.moderator_quote: the database covers 46.5% of links posted by members of the US
estimates.notes: Whole-period average (2016-01-01 to 2022-03-16); year=2022 is the end of the collection window, not a single year of behaviour. TIME SERIES COLLAPSED: the paper's temporal breakdown gives Republicans 2.4% +/- 0.2% in 2016-2018 rising to 5.5% +/- 0.7% in 2020-2022, so this 3.86% average sits between a lower early level and a higher recent one. DENOMINATOR AMBIGUITY (the reason confidence is medium, applies to every row here): the paper says only 'the overall proportion of links that point to domains that are considered untrustworthy' while separately noting that NewsGuard covers 46.5% of US links. If the proportion is computed over all extracted links, unrated links sit in the denominator and the estimate is conservative; if it is computed over rated links only, the true share is roughly double (and denom_scope would be news_diet rather than all_media). The robustness check with an independently compiled domain list gives 5.9% (2016-2018) to 11.3% (2020-2022) for Republicans, i.e. the level is sensitive to the list used. Coverage caveats: only the most recent 3,200 tweets per account were scraped (the supplement reports an all-tweets analysis with similar results), and 61.7% of relevant members of Congress were captured. ground_truth coded domain_list because classification is at domain level from a curated list; 'fact_checker' is defensible given the paper's own wording. QUOTE NOTE: this PDF renders as two interleaved columns, so no full sentence exists as one contiguous span in the text file; the source_quote is an exact single-line span. The full sentence reads: "Overall, Republicans share 9.1 times more links to websites considered unstrustworthy than Democrats (Republicans 3.86%, Democrats 0.43%, difference 3.44%, 1.65 SD). For Germany, members of the CDU/CSU post 6.3 times more links to such websites than members of the SPD (CDU/CSU 0.18%, SPD 0.03%, difference 0.15%, 0.04 SD). For the United Kingdom, members of the Tories post 4.7 times more links to untrustworthy domains than members of the Labour Party (Tory 0.25%, Labour 0.05%, difference 0.19%, 0.08 SD)."

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted: (1) Mean NewsGuard SCORES of shared links (Republicans 89.9 -> 85.2; Democrats 94.2 -> 94.8; AfD 83.9 -> 83.0; CDU/CSU 92.2 -> 91.6; DUP 83.4 -> 85.6; UK Conservatives 89.1 -> 88.2) - these are scale means, not shares of links, so no row (value_kind scale_score would apply if the project wanted them; §1 excludes scale means with no share). (2) The temporal sub-windows for the US and the AfD (Republicans 2.4% -> 5.5%; Democrats 0.4% -> 0.4%) - collapsed into the whole-period rows per §2 and recorded in each row's notes; the AfD row is the exception because no whole-period AfD average is published. (3) The robustness-check values from the independently compiled domain list (Republicans 5.9% -> 11.3%; Democrats 0.8% -> 0.3%) - these are the same measure under a different ground-truth list, so they would be definition_variant rows; I left them out because they are only reported for the two US parties and only per sub-window, never for the whole period, so a variant row could not be matched to the kept rows. An adjudicator who wants a definition_variant row should note it would roughly double the US Republican figure, which is the single most important sensitivity in this paper. (4) The statement that the conservative parties in Germany and the UK post more untrustworthy links than their counterparts on the left but about half as many as US Democrats - a comparison, no new value. (5) 'The proportion of links to untrustworthy domains of all other parties in Germany and the United Kingdom is similar to the proportion posted by Democrats and does not change over time' - qualitative, no values for the remaining parties. (6) Database/coverage statistics (6,860 English and 145 German domains indexed; 62.8% and 74.5% trustworthy; 46.5%/58.8%/39.2% link coverage; 61.7%/65.7%/78.6% politician coverage) - method characteristics, not prevalence, but recorded in the denominators. (7) Figures cited from other studies (refs 6, 10, 11, 13) are excluded by R8. Main judgement calls for the adjudicator: (a) whether the denominator is ALL extracted links or only NewsGuard-rated links - this changes every value by roughly a factor of two and drives my denom_scope=all_media choice; (b) ground_truth domain_list vs fact_checker (the authors call NewsGuard 'professional fact checkers' but rate domains, not items); (c) keeping seven party-level rows rather than one per country - justified because §2 explicitly permits subgroup rows when they are the paper's headline, which the party contrast is, and no country-level pooled value is published.

rob.design: Observational link-sharing analysis of 3.4 million tweets. Corpora: the most recent 3,200 tweets per account scraped via the Twitter API for former and present members of the US Congress (1,023 handles, 61.7% of members of the 114th-117th Congress), the German parliament (822 handles, 65.7%) and the British parliament (726 handles, 78.6%), covering 2016-01-01 to 2022-03-16; retweets and tweets not in the country's national language excluded, leaving 1,694,403 (US), 754,233 (DE) and 960,114 (UK) tweets. All external URLs extracted, shorteners expanded, and each domain matched to NewsGuard nutrition scores (0-100; <60 = 'not trustworthy'); NewsGuard indexed 6,860 English and 145 German domains as of March 2022 and covers only 46.5% / 58.8% / 39.2% of the links in the three corpora. Source-level rather than item-level classification, so a true story on a low-rated domain counts as untrustworthy and vice versa. Validation: authors checked NewsGuard for missing major outlets and their political bias, reproduced the main result with an independently compiled domain list (which yields substantially higher levels), and report an all-tweets (not 3,200-capped) analysis in the supplement with similar results; confidence intervals by bootstrap over 1,000 iterations; monthly values smoothed with a 3-month rolling average. Authors' own limitation: the German and UK figures rest on very low absolute counts of untrustworthy links. Reproduction materials (tweet IDs, party labels, independent domain list, code) are public at OSF; the NewsGuard database is proprietary. NOTE on quotes: the available text rendering interleaves the article's two columns line by line, so item6_quote and item10_quote are exact single-line spans rather than whole sentences; the reconstructed sentences appear in the row notes.
